summary: Fire lookout station on Ensign Peak in Salt Lake City, seen in a 1948 newspaper account; listed as abandoned; the peak is now a city park.

facts.status_note: Listed as abandoned; no source says when or whether anything was removed

access.note: Ensign Peak Nature Park, owned by the city; a popular trail leads to the summit

visit.trail_note: Ensign Peak Trail, a 0.47-mile hike to the summit

events.note: Fire lookout station in use on the peak in July 1948; a water department ranger visited it on his rounds, per the Telegram account

evidence.supports: Ensign Peak is a hill just north of downtown Salt Lake City
evidence.quote: Ensign Peak is the summit of a hill just north of downtown Salt Lake City

evidence.supports: fire lookout station atop Ensign Peak in 1948, a two-mile uphill hike from the boy's home
evidence.quote: By noon, he had reached the fire lookout station atop Ensign peak, a two-mile uphill hike from his home.

evidence.supports: water department ranger drove up to the lookout
evidence.quote: Shortly afterward, Dick Raybould, ranger for the Salt Lake City water department, drove up to the Ensign peak lookout.

evidence.supports: the ranger found a visitor occupying the lookout station
ranger carried on with his duties after identifying himself
evidence.quote: After he had properly identified himself, Mr. Raybould was allowed to continue his duties with the junior ranger.

corrections.why: The Forest Fire Lookout Association's Utah list gives Ensign Peak as Abandoned. No source we read says the station was removed.

notes_for_editor: Only one detailed source: a 1948 Salt Lake Telegram account quoted on the Forest Lookouts site. No build or removal date found. The brief's 'gone' is not supported; the FFLOS list says Abandoned. Do not confuse with the Walker Bank Building lookout (1939 to about 1948), which is a different site.
